lead: Both readings today ask the same question: who is Jesus? Paul answers with an early hymn of the Church: “He was revealed in flesh, vindicated in spirit, seen by angels.” In John the question is put to Jesus directly, “Who are you?”, and he answers that it will become plain when he is lifted up on the cross. The Church, Paul says, is the household that holds up this truth for the world to see. The key words are mystery and lifted up.

r.h: The pillar and bulwark of the truth
set: The First Letter to Timothy is written to Paul's young co-worker, left in charge of the Church at Ephesus (1:3). It gives instructions on prayer, on the qualities of bishops and deacons (3:1–13), and on the life of the community. Many scholars think that the Pastoral Letters (1 and 2 Timothy, Titus) were written in Paul's name by a disciple after his death; others hold that they come from Paul himself, late in his life. Either way, the Church receives them as inspired Scripture.
Today's three verses are the hinge of the letter. Paul explains why he writes, and then breaks into what most scholars take to be a hymn or confession already in use in the Church's worship.
str: vv. 14–15: why he writes: so that Timothy may know how to behave in the household of God.
v. 16: the hymn of the mystery, in six short lines.
¶ The lines come in pairs that join earth and heaven: flesh and spirit, angels and nations, the world and glory.
kw: Not a building but a family. The same letter asks that a bishop manage his own household well, “for if someone does not know how to manage his own household, how can he take care of God's church?” (3:5). The Church is God's family, with its order, its table and its care for the weak.

A pillar holds something up so that it can be seen; a bulwark (foundation, support) keeps it firm. The temple of Artemis at Ephesus was famous for its many pillars. Paul says the true pillar is the Church of the living God, and what she holds up is the truth.
Literally “the mystery of godliness” or “of devotion”. In Paul a mystery is not a riddle but God's plan, once hidden and now revealed in Christ (Colossians 1:26).
vv: you may know how one ought to behave in the household of God, which is the church of the living God, the pillar and bulwark of the truth.
Conduct comes first. Before he speaks of doctrine, Paul speaks of how people behave in God's house. Truth and life belong together.
Without any doubt, the mystery of our religion is great:
The Greek word translated “without any doubt” means “by common confession”: what follows is what all believers confess together.
He was revealed in flesh, vindicated in spirit, seen by angels,

The best and oldest manuscripts begin “who was revealed”; some later manuscripts read “God was revealed in flesh”. Both say the same faith: the one revealed in the flesh is the eternal Son. “Vindicated in spirit” points to the Resurrection, in which the Spirit showed him to be righteous.
ch: The Catechism quotes this verse when it speaks of the Church as the guardian of revealed truth: the Church, “the pillar and bulwark of the truth”, faithfully guards the faith handed on once for all to the saints (CCC 171). It also quotes the hymn of verse 16, “the mystery of our religion”, and sees in it the heart of faith in the true Incarnation of the Son of God (CCC 463). The Church does not stand above the truth; she serves it, holds it up and keeps it safe.

r.h: When you have lifted up the Son of Man
set: Jesus is teaching in the temple in Jerusalem during the feast of Tabernacles (7:2, 7:14; 8:20). The conversation in chapter 8 is tense. In John's Gospel “the Jews” in such scenes usually means the religious authorities who opposed Jesus; here the questioners are the Pharisees of 8:13. John himself, like Jesus and the first disciples, was a Jew, and today's passage ends with many of the hearers coming to faith (8:30).
Just before, Jesus has said: “you will die in your sins unless you believe that I am he” (8:24). The question “Who are you?” follows from that.
str: vv. 25–27: “Who are you?”; Jesus speaks of the one who sent him; they do not understand.
vv. 28–29: when the Son of Man is lifted up, they will know that “I am he”.
kw: Literally “I am”. In the Greek Old Testament God speaks of himself with these words: “that you may know and believe me and understand that I am he” (Isaiah 43:10). Jesus uses the same words of himself (8:24, 28, 58).
The word means both to raise up and to exalt. In John it always points to the cross, where Jesus is raised up and glorified at the same time (3:14; 12:32–33).
One of John's favourite ways of speaking of the Father. Everything Jesus says and does comes from the Father who sent him.
vv: They said to him, “Who are you?”

Jesus's answer in the Greek is one of the hardest phrases in John. The NRSV renders it as a question, “Why do I speak to you at all?”; other translations, like the POC, read it as “What I have told you from the beginning”. Either way, Jesus will not give a new title. He has already told them.
When you have lifted up the Son of Man, then you will realize that I am he,
A startling promise: the moment of his deepest humiliation will be the moment his identity shines out. At the cross the centurion in Mark says, “Truly this man was God's Son!” (Mark 15:39).
he has not left me alone, for I always do what is pleasing to him.
Even on the cross Jesus is not abandoned by the Father. His whole life is obedience, and in that obedience he is never alone.
ch: The Catechism quotes verse 28 when it teaches about the divine name. God revealed himself to Moses as “I AM”; Jesus reveals that he himself bears that name, and that this will be seen when he is lifted up (CCC 211). The Church therefore reads this passage as a revelation of the divinity of Christ, which is shown most clearly not in power but in the cross.

rite: The Panchangam remembers today St Justin, philosopher and martyr. Born about the year 100 at Flavia Neapolis in Samaria, he searched for truth among the philosophers and found it in Christ. He opened a school in Rome and was beheaded there with several companions around 165. His First Apology gives the oldest full description of the Sunday Eucharist, which the Catechism quotes at length (CCC 1345). Justin is a fitting saint for these readings: he went looking for the answer to the question “Who are you?” and found it in the crucified Lord.
study: Paul calls the Church “the household of God”. How do I behave in God's house, and in my own home, so that the truth can be seen?
Jesus says that people will know who he is when he is lifted up. What does the cross teach me about who Jesus is?
